scenes.title: 2011 Columbia-Harvard Computer Lab: Typing 40 Trivia Facts Into 'Saved' Folder vs 'Erased' Screen
scenes.era: 2011, Harvard & Columbia cognitive psychology testing suite

layout.description: Sunlit wood-paneled university testing room with two desktop stations: at Station A, a 49-year-old volunteer watches typed trivia slide into a yellow desktop file folder icon and relaxes back; at Station B, a volunteer sees the typed entry vanish cleanly and leans forward rehearsing the fact.

positions.who: 49-year-old adult volunteer (in collared Oxford shirt and olive knit vest)
positions.where: seated at the wooden testing desk typing trivia statements on a mechanical keyboard before facing a blank sheet recall test
positions.facing: seated facing desktop monitor and researcher

positions.who: Betsy Sparrow (researcher in tailored navy blazer holding folder-recall scoring sheet)
positions.where: standing beside the desk comparing weak content recall against pinpoint folder-location recall
positions.facing: angled toward the volunteer and desktop station

props.name: desktop computer keyboard and color-tabbed physical manila folder tray
props.period_detail: 2011 Experiment 2 & 3 saved-vs-erased and 6-folder location memory test
props.physical_behavior: State-A fingers finish typing trivia card and drop it into labeled folder slot -> State-B volunteer points straight to the exact folder tab while shrugging blankly at what the card inside actually said

props.name: surprise blank recall pad and uncapped fountain pen
props.period_detail: measures verbatim statement recall (29% erased vs 19% saved)
props.physical_behavior: State-A saved-condition pad sits half-empty at 19% -> State-B erased-condition volunteer writes briskly reaching 29% recall

actions.verb_sequence: types the final keystroke, watches the file drop into the saved folder -> taps temple blankly on the fact quiz yet points unhesitatingly to the exact folder slot
lifts the folder tab revealing the brain stored the filing address instead of the sentence

reactions.reaction: laughs in recognition realizing 'I know right where it's saved, just not what it says!'
nods marking transactive external memory offloading

scenes.wardrobe: Smart-casual olive vest over white Oxford shirt; tailored navy jacket on researcher.
scenes.lighting: Clean high-key afternoon campus window light.
scenes.recognition_hook: Promise the brain a file is saved, and recall drops from 29% to 19%—while memory for which folder holds it stays razor-sharp.

key_visual.description: an adult volunteer at a wooden university desk pointing confidently to a specific file folder tab while pausing over a surprise memory pad beside a researcher

scenes.title: Outdoor Sunlit Sculpture Courtyard Tour: Point-and-Shoot Whole Photo vs Pausing & Zooming In (Henkel 2014)
scenes.era: Modern sunlit outdoor museum sculpture courtyard

layout.description: Sunlit open-air limestone museum courtyard lined with classical bronze and marble sculptures under blue sky.

positions.who: 56-year-old museum visitor (in light linen jacket carrying compact digital camera)
positions.where: walking past a classical bronze courtyard statue—first snapping a hasty one-second wide photo, then stopping at the next sculpture to observe closely and zoom the lens barrel onto carved hands

props.name: compact zoom camera and classical courtyard bronze sculpture
props.period_detail: Linda Henkel's 2014 point-and-shoot vs optical-zoom encoding test
props.physical_behavior: State-A hasty one-handed wide shutter click walking right past -> State-B two-handed steady optical zoom ring turn studying carved detail for five full seconds

actions.verb_sequence: lowers the camera for five quiet seconds to take in the sunlit bronze sculpture with naked eyes -> gently twists the zoom ring onto a single detail

reactions.reaction: warm, attentive smile absorbing the real moment instead of outsourcing it

scenes.wardrobe: Light sand linen jacket over navy polo shirt.
scenes.recognition_hook: Snap a lazy wide photo and your hippocampus skips encoding; pause five seconds or zoom onto one detail and your memory keeps the whole scene.

spatial_contrast_spec.landmark_or_object_a: Sculpture A photographed in one hasty second and immediately forgotten down the gallery path
spatial_contrast_spec.landmark_or_object_b: Sculpture B observed directly with naked eyes or zoomed in closely, locking full detail into memory
spatial_contrast_spec.cut_a_landmark_drone: Fast 3D aerial sweep over a sunlit university museum courtyard descending into an open gallery walkway
spatial_contrast_spec.cut_b_topdown_3d_arrow: Top-down courtyard floorplan where a #FF2525 3D volumetric arrow zigzags from sculpture pedestal to pedestal—fading on hasty shutter clicks and glowing bright on paused eye contact
